meta.title: Odaiba Statue of Liberty – Free Visit, History & Access
meta.description: Explore Tokyo's Statue of Liberty in Odaiba. Free admission, directions from Daiba Station, history, photo spots and Rainbow Bridge views.

nonprofitBanner.text: This is a non-profit, independent guide compiled by enthusiastic travellers, aiming to give you the most objective advice for visiting the Statue of Liberty Odaiba.

mission.title: Our Mission
mission.text: So that every visitor to Japan leaves Odaiba without regret, we have gathered these scattered official details — only to give you the purest possible visit.

entryAnswers.title: Do you need tickets for the Odaiba Statue of Liberty? No — it's free.
entryAnswers.subtitle: It is an open-air monument in a public seaside park: no ticket office, no gate, no booking and no closing time.

items.a: No. There is no ticket counter and no entrance gate, so there is nothing to buy and nothing to print. Walk straight onto the seaside promenade and look up.
The statue is open 24 hours a day, every day of the year. Early morning and late evening are the quietest; the hour around sunset is the busiest.
At the end of the seaside promenade in Odaiba Kaihin Park — about a 5-minute walk from Daiba Station (Exit A) or Odaiba-Kaihinkoen Station.

items.q: When is the best time to visit?
items.a: Around sunset and just after dark, when the Rainbow Bridge lights up behind the statue — the classic Odaiba photo.

hero.title: Statue of Liberty Odaiba
hero.subtitle: A 1/7-scale replica of New York's Statue of Liberty, standing quietly on the Odaiba waterfront along Tokyo Bay. It was installed in 1998 during the 'Year of France in Japan' as a temporary exhibit, and proved so popular it remained a permanent Odaiba landmark. With its verdigris-green figure framed by the Rainbow Bridge and Tokyo Bay, it is Odaiba's most recognisable landmark — and a free, always-open civic icon.

intro.title: Discover the Statue of Liberty Odaiba
intro.description: The Statue of Liberty Odaiba stands on the Odaiba waterfront along Tokyo Bay as a 1/7-scale replica of the original in New York. It was installed in 1998 during the 'Year of France in Japan' as a temporary exhibit, and proved so popular that it was made permanent in 2000. About 12 metres tall and finished in the same verdigris green as the New York original, it faces Tokyo Bay and the Rainbow Bridge — one of Odaiba's signature landmarks and the first sight many visitors see from the water bus or the Yurikamome train.

visitGuide.title: Visitor Guide
visitGuide.description: As an open-air statue in a public waterfront park, the Statue of Liberty Odaiba can be visited free of charge at any hour, with no ticket and no crowd control.
items: Allow 30 minutes to an hour: stroll Odaiba Kaihin Park, photograph the statue with the Rainbow Bridge, or catch the backlit silhouette at dusk.
The statue sits inside the open Odaiba Seaside Park, within walking distance of the shopping districts (Aqua City, DECKS, DiverCity) — easy to combine in one trip.
It is windy and lightly shaded by the bay: bring water, a hat and sunscreen; winter feels noticeably colder.
From Shimbashi Station, take the Yurikamome Line about 15 minutes to Daiba Station, then walk roughly 5 minutes.

alsoKnownAs.title: Highlights
items: An official 1/7-scale replica of New York's Statue of Liberty
A 1/7-scale replica installed in 1998 during the Year of France in Japan
About 12 m tall, verdigris green, framed perfectly by the Rainbow Bridge

transportSection.title: Driver & Guide · How to Reach the Statue of Liberty Odaiba
transportSection.subtitle: Whether by air, train, public transit, car, taxi, bike or water bus, each option is detailed below, with parking and driver FAQs.
transportSection.overviewText: Tokyo is reached via Narita or Haneda airports, the Tokaido Shinkansen or highway buses. Once in the city, Odaiba lies on reclaimed land in Tokyo Bay, Minato Ward. The most convenient rail lines are the Yurikamome (from Shimbashi) and the Rinkai Line (Tokyo Teleport Station); from either, a short walk brings you to the statue.
transportSection.overviewText2: The statue is free and open 24 hours, at the end of the Odaiba Kaihin Park seaside promenade, framed with the Rainbow Bridge and the Tokyo Bay skyline. Plan your transport, parking and walking route together to avoid on-site confusion and congestion.
transportSection.arrivalTitle: Know this before you set out
arrivalItems: The statue is on the flat seaside promenade of Odaiba Kaihin Park, a 5–10 minute walk from Daiba or Tokyo Teleport stations.
There is no dedicated statue parking; use paid lots at nearby commercial facilities such as Aqua City, DECKS or DiverCity.
Weekends and holidays get crowded, especially at dusk and for night views — consider off-peak times.

modes.label: By Air (Haneda / Narita)
modes.title: From the two airports
modes.description: Best for overseas and long-distance domestic travellers; Haneda is closer, Narita has more flights.
details: Haneda: Tokyo Monorail to Hamamatsucho, transfer to the Yurikamome to Daiba Station — about 40 minutes, roughly ¥700.
Narita: Narita Express (N'EX) to Tokyo Station then transfer to the Yurikamome; or Keisei Skyliner to central Tokyo then transfer — about 1.5 hours, roughly ¥2,500–3,000.
Both airports have taxis and limousine buses, but crossing the bay to Odaiba is costly and prone to Rainbow Bridge congestion — not recommended unless necessary.

steps.t: After leaving the airport, follow signs to central-Tokyo rail lines.
Alight at Daiba Station (Exit A) or Odaiba-Kaihinkoen, then walk 5–10 minutes.

modes.label: Train / Private Rail
modes.title: Yurikamome · Daiba Station
modes.description: The most convenient and recommended way to the statue.
details: From Shimbashi, take the Yurikamome (fully driverless) about 15 minutes to Daiba Station, Exit A, then walk about 5 minutes.
Alternatively, alight at Odaiba-Kaihinkoen Station and follow the waterfront promenade about 5 minutes, with the statue and Rainbow Bridge already in view.
The Yurikamome accepts Suica / PASMO IC cards directly — no ticket queues.

steps.t: At Shimbashi, find the dedicated Yurikamome gates (a different level from JR).
Take a Toyosu-bound train, about 6 stops to Daiba Station.
Exit A and follow the seaside-park signs on foot.

modes.label: Public Transit (Rinkai Line)
modes.title: Rinkai Line · Tokyo Teleport Stn
modes.description: Most direct from Shinjuku, Shibuya and Ikebukuro.
details: Take the Rinkai Line to Tokyo Teleport Station, then walk about 10 minutes.
The Rinkai Line runs through to JR Saikyo Line, so no transfer from Shinjuku or Ikebukuro; from Shibuya, change once at Shinjuku or Osaki.
Tokyo Teleport Station has elevators — easier than the sloping Daiba Station if you have large luggage or children/seniors.

steps.t: From Shinjuku/Ikebukuro, take a Saikyo Line train (through-serviced to the Rinkai Line).
Alight at Tokyo Teleport Station and follow the 'Kaihin Koen' exit.
Walk along the flat promenade about 10 minutes.

modes.label: By Car (Parking)
modes.title: Via the Rainbow Bridge · Nearby Parking
modes.description: Good with luggage, children/seniors, or for a bay-circling drive. No statue-only lot — use nearby commercial facilities.
details: Navigate to 'Odaiba Kaihin Park' or 'Aqua City Odaiba' and cross the toll Rainbow Bridge (about ¥700 one-way for a standard car) into Odaiba.
Daiba shopping mall / Kaihin Park paid lots, Aqua City, DECKS and DiverCity all offer paid parking; weekends and holidays fill up fast — arrive early or reserve.
The Rainbow Bridge upper deck is for cars, the lower deck for pedestrians and cyclists; drivers use the upper car deck and pay on crossing.

steps.t: Set your nav destination to the Aqua City Odaiba or DECKS Tokyo Beach parking.
Cross the Rainbow Bridge upper deck into Odaiba, following signs to the mall parking.
Park, then walk 5–10 minutes to the statue; avoid the dusk peak to save time hunting for a space.

modes.label: Taxi / Rideshare
modes.title: Door-to-door
modes.description: Easiest with luggage, children/seniors, or late-night arrival.
details: From central Tokyo (Ginza, Shimbashi) a taxi to Odaiba takes about 20–30 minutes, roughly ¥3,000–5,000 plus the Rainbow Bridge toll.
Ask the driver to drop you at the transfer drop-off point by Daiba Station (Yurikamome) — about a 5-minute walk, avoiding parking hassle.
In rain/snow or weekend evenings, wait times are longer; leave a buffer and book via a local taxi app.

modes.label: Cycling / Water Bus
modes.title: Waterfront rides & sea routes
modes.description: The most relaxing, photo-friendly way to enjoy the city.
details: Ride the Tokyo Bay waterfront cycle path to link Odaiba's sights; shared bikes (e.g. Docomo Bike Share) are available at some piers.
Take a Tokyo Cruise water bus (Hotaluna / Emeraldas) from Asakusa or Hinode Pier to Odaiba, viewing the statue and Rainbow Bridge from the bay.
The Rainbow Bridge lower deck has dedicated pedestrian and cycle lanes — walking or cycling across is an experience in itself.

modes.label: On Foot
modes.title: Arrive by the waterfront walk
modes.description: If you're already in Odaiba, walking is the most natural way to arrive.
details: From Daiba Station, about 5 minutes toward Kaihin Park; from Tokyo Teleport, about 10 minutes — all flat and accessible.
From DECKS, Aqua City or DiverCity, follow the seaside promenade; benches and viewing decks line the way.
The promenade gets busy at dusk — keep an eye on children and belongings.

parking.title: Parking Overview (for drivers)
parking.note: The statue has no own parking lot. The options below are the nearest major paid lots; rates and availability vary by season and time — please follow on-site signs.
parking.disclaimer: Street parking is restricted along the waterfront — use paid lots and public transit. Rates and restrictions may change — please check posted notices.

driverFaq.q: Is there parking near the Statue of Liberty Odaiba?
driverFaq.a: Odaiba Kaihin Park and shopping malls (Aqua City, DECKS Tokyo Beach) offer paid parking. We suggest parking near the Yurikamome Daiba Station or the Rinkai Tokyo Teleport Station, then walking.

driverFaq.q: What is the nearest parking option?
driverFaq.a: The Daiba shopping mall / Kaihin Park paid lots, about a 200 m walk to the statue.
Limited — the waterfront mainly uses paid lots and public transit; avoid long street parking.

driverFaq.q: Is the Statue of Liberty Odaiba good to drive to?
driverFaq.a: Driving is possible, but weekends and holidays bring Rainbow Bridge and Odaiba congestion — the Yurikamome is usually faster. Unless you need parking, public transit is advised.
Strongly. Daiba Station (Yurikamome) is about a 5-minute walk; Tokyo Big Sight (Rinkai Line) is also walkable. Address: 1 Chome-4-2 Daiba, Minato City, Tokyo.

driverFaq.q: What is the best route to get there?
driverFaq.a: Public transit is best: Daiba Station (Yurikamome) ~5 min walk, or Tokyo Teleport Station (Rinkai Line) ~10 min walk. By car, cross the Rainbow Bridge and park at a nearby mall, then walk.

localTips: Light is softest at dusk, when Lady Liberty and the Rainbow Bridge glow against a golden sky.
The statue is open 24 hours; the illuminated Odaiba at night is equally charming for an evening stroll.
Combine with nearby Aqua City and DiverCity (Unicorn Gundam); malls offer restrooms and food.

bestTime.title: Best Time to Arrive
bestTime.text: Although it is open 24 hours, we recommend arriving about an hour before sunset — you'll capture three views in one trip: daytime, golden hour and night lights. It is the lowest-cost, highest-return strategy.

officialManagement.title: About the Statue
officialManagement.text: The Statue of Liberty Odaiba is a public open-air monument within Odaiba Kaihin Park, maintained under the 'Umi-no-Koen' (sea park) system operated by Tokyo Port Authority (Tokyo Port & Harbor Corporation) under the Tokyo Metropolitan Government. As a free, publicly accessible waterfront space, it offers residents and visitors a place to enjoy Tokyo Bay, take photos and relax, and ranks among the most representative landscapes of the Odaiba waterfront subcentre.

knowledge.title: History & Significance of the Statue of Liberty Odaiba

sections.title: Origins: the Year of France, 1998
sections.content: The Statue of Liberty Odaiba was installed in 1998 (Heisei 10) during the 'Année de la France au Japon' (Year of France in Japan) as a temporary exhibit. So beloved by the public and visitors, it remained a permanent fixture of the Odaiba waterfront.

sections.title: Why Japan? A symbol of Franco-Japanese friendship
sections.content: New York's Statue of Liberty was itself a gift from France to the United States, symbolising liberty and the bond between the two nations. Odaiba's replica continues that thread — it, too, is a cross-border emblem of friendship, carrying the long artistic, cultural and diplomatic ties between Japan and France, and lending the shores of Tokyo Bay a touch of French romance.

sections.title: The bloodline of the New York original
sections.content: The prototype of Odaiba's statue is the Liberty Enlightening the World erected in New York Harbor in 1886, sculpted by the French artist Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi. Its internal steel framework was designed by Gustave Eiffel — of Eiffel Tower fame — a masterpiece joining engineering and art.

sections.title: Form & Symbolism
sections.content: Every detail carries meaning: the crown's seven spikes stand for the seven continents and seven seas; the raised torch represents liberty lighting the world; the tablet bears the date of American independence, 'JULY IV MDCCLXXVI' (July 4, 1776); and the broken chains at the feet symbolise freedom from oppression.

sections.title: A 1/7-scale replica
sections.content: The Odaiba version stands about 12 metres tall — roughly 1/7 of the New York original (about 93 m including pedestal). Though smaller, its crown, torch and tablet are proportionally faithful, and it is painted the same verdigris green as New York, so from afar it is almost indistinguishable.

sections.title: A landmark of the Odaiba waterfront
sections.content: Odaiba began as a battery island at the end of the Edo period and later became a waterfront subcentre through Tokyo Bay land reclamation. Today it gathers seaside parks, commercial facilities and the Rainbow Bridge; the Statue of Liberty stands at the end of the promenade, forming a classic tableau with the skyline and the bridge across Tokyo Bay.

sections.title: Odaiba's green landmark
sections.content: As free, open public art, the Statue of Liberty Odaiba is now the go-to spot for photos, sunsets and night views. It is both Odaiba's visual signature and a unique thread connecting the cultures and emotions of New York, Paris and Tokyo.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: Odaiba's Statue of Liberty is a 1/7-scale replica of the New York original, even reproducing its verdigris patina — and the original's internal steel frame was designed by Gustave Eiffel, of Eiffel Tower fame.

reviews.featuredSubtitle: A few short lines that capture the spirit of the Statue of Liberty Odaiba.

featured.text: I thought only New York had one — didn't expect to pose with 'Lady Liberty' on Tokyo Bay.
At dusk the statue and Rainbow Bridge light up together — Odaiba's most romantic moment.
A free open-air landmark you pass on a stroll; the kids were thrilled.

items.name: Kenji T.
items.text: A pleasant surprise while walking Odaiba Kaihin Park. Smaller than New York but the verdigris green with the Rainbow Bridge is very photogenic — strongly recommend coming at dusk.

items.name: Aiko M.
items.text: Spotted it from the Yurikamome train. Free and open 24 hours, beautifully lit at night — perfect for an after-dinner walk.

items.name: Hiroshi K.
items.text: Meaningful as a symbol of Franco-Japanese friendship, with many photo angles. Busy on weekends; weekdays are calmer.

items.name: Yuki S.
items.text: Easy to combine with nearby Aqua City and DiverCity; malls have restrooms and food, so it's relaxed even with kids.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Practical information on facilities, the statue's history and planning your visit to the Statue of Liberty Odaiba.

items.q: Is there parking nearby? How much does it cost?
items.a: The statue itself has no dedicated parking, but nearby commercial facilities — Aqua City, DECKS Tokyo Beach, DiverCity Tokyo Plaza — all have paid parking just a few minutes' walk away. Rates are typically hourly; they fill quickly on weekends, holidays and for night views, so arrive early or prefer public transit.

items.q: Can wheelchairs or strollers get close?
items.a: Yes. The statue sits in Odaiba Kaihin Park on an open seaside promenade that is completely flat with no steps, so wheelchairs, strollers and mobility aids move easily; accessible ramps and restrooms are along the way.

items.q: Are there restrooms or food nearby?
items.a: There are no standalone restrooms at the statue, but Aqua City, DECKS and DiverCity are a few minutes' walk away, with public restrooms, cafés, restaurants and convenience stores — so grabbing food and facilities is very convenient.

items.q: What is this statue for, and why is it in Tokyo?
items.a: It is a 1/7-scale replica of New York's Statue of Liberty, installed in 1998 during the 'Year of France in Japan' as a temporary exhibit. So popular with visitors, it became a permanent fixture of the Odaiba waterfront.

items.q: How is it related to the one in New York?
items.a: Odaiba's version faithfully reproduces the proportions and form of the New York original, even recreating its verdigris patina. The New York statue was created by Bartholdi with an internal steel frame by Gustave Eiffel, dedicated in 1886 as a French gift to the United States — Odaiba's replica continues that cross-border bond.
No. The Statue of Liberty Odaiba is an open-air monument in a public seaside park — free and open around the clock, with no ticket office or gate (nearby mall facilities are separate).

items.q: How long does a visit take?
items.a: A typical visit lasts 30 minutes to an hour: arrive, take photos, stroll the promenade, perhaps rest on a bench. Allow extra time if you also explore Aqua City or DiverCity (Unicorn Gundam).

items.q: Can I go in bad weather?
items.a: Yes — it is an outdoor public space, visitable in any weather. But it is windy by the bay and lightly shaded in summer, so bring water and sun protection; winter and after rain feel colder and paths may be slippery — dress for wind and warmth.

items.q: After visiting, what else do you recommend nearby?
items.a: The statue is right by the Rainbow Bridge and Tokyo Bay waterfront, within walking distance of Aqua City, DECKS Tokyo Beach, DiverCity Tokyo Plaza (Unicorn Gundam) and the Fuji Television building. A little further are Odaiba Kaihin Park, Tokyo Big Sight, and the water-bus route to Asakusa.

scienceArt.title: Design & Symbolism: Liberty, Enlightenment & French Aesthetics
scienceArt.subtitle: The Statue of Liberty Odaiba is more than a replica — it is a public symbol packed with political meaning, engineering wisdom and artistic language. Two dimensions help you read it.

scienceMuseum.name: Form & Symbolism
scienceMuseum.role: Liberty, enlightenment and French aesthetics combined
scienceMuseum.highlight: The crown's seven spikes stand for the seven continents and seven seas, proclaiming liberty for all the world; the raised torch is the light of liberty illuminating the world; the tablet bears the date of American independence, 'July 4, 1776'; the broken chains at the feet symbolise freedom from oppression. The verdigris green comes from oxidised copper — 'the colour of liberty' bestowed by time.
points: Crown's seven rays: universal liberty across every continent and ocean.
Torch & tablet: 'independence' and 'enlightenment' frozen in light and date.
Broken chains & patina: a metaphor of emancipation, and a classic hue aged over a century.

artMuseum.name: The Original & Its Lineage
artMuseum.role: A gift of friendship across the seas
artMuseum.highlight: The New York original was sculpted by French artist Bartholdi, with an internal steel frame by Gustave Eiffel of Eiffel Tower fame, dedicated in 1886 as France's gift to the United States. Odaiba's replica continues the bond between France–Japan and France–America.
points: Bartholdi: personifying 'Liberty' in the language of classical sculpture.
Eiffel: solving the structural challenge of a giant statue with a steel skeleton — an engineering marvel.
Dedicated 1886: the Statue of Liberty becomes a global emblem of liberty from New York Harbor onward.

outdoorMuseum.title: Photo & Viewing Guide: Best Shots of the Statue of Liberty Odaiba
outdoorMuseum.subtitle: As a highly photogenic landmark, a few structured vantage points and timing tips greatly boost both the utility and the beauty of your photos.

items.name: The Classic Front Shot
items.background: A level, head-on view from the promenade is the safest angle to recreate the 'New York' composition. With Tokyo Bay and sky as background, you get a clean, symmetrical full-body portrait.
points: Centre the statue and use the open water as negative space to highlight the verdigris subject.
Crouch low and shoot upward to lengthen the figure and emphasise the crown and torch.

items.name: Framed with the Rainbow Bridge
items.location: Waterfront platform to the statue's right
items.background: Move to the right of the statue to bring the Rainbow Bridge into frame. The red-and-white suspension bridge against the green statue creates a striking colour contrast — Odaiba's most recognisable postcard view.
points: Use the Rainbow Bridge as a diagonal lead-in line to add depth and tension.
A telephoto lens compresses the scene so the statue and bridge feel 'closer'.

items.name: Dusk & Night Views
items.background: Around sunset the backlight gilds the statue; after dark the Rainbow Bridge lights up and the statue glows in the blue hour against the city — the most atmospheric moment.
points: Shoot in the blue hour (20–30 min after sunset) when sky and lights are balanced.
A tripod with long exposure captures light trails of traffic on the bridge.

items.name: Tokyo Bay Reflection
items.background: Approaching Odaiba by water bus from Asakusa or Hinode, you see the statue at eye level from the bay; on calm days the statue and Rainbow Bridge reflect on Tokyo Bay — a unique sea-level perspective.
points: Ride the upper deck and shoot past the railings to avoid crowds.
Mornings bring calmer water and more complete reflections.

education.title: Why a Statue of Liberty in Odaiba? (The Social Meaning of Public Art)
education.subtitle: A statue from New York, born in Paris, rooted on Tokyo Bay — behind it lie multiple narratives of city, culture and diplomacy.

points.title: Making Franco-Japanese friendship tangible
points.text: In 1998, the 'Year of France in Japan' brought the Statue of Liberty replica to Odaiba as a public artwork. It turns cultural exchange into a touchable, photo-friendly public landscape, continuing the ties between Japan and France.

points.title: Public art & urban renewal
points.text: Odaiba — once industrial reclaimed land — was transformed into a citizens' and visitors' waterfront leisure zone through seaside parks, commercial facilities and iconic public art. The Statue of Liberty is a microcosm of this 'culture activates urban space' strategy.

points.title: Connecting cross-cultural symbols
points.text: The same statue links New York (liberty), Paris (creation and gift) and Tokyo (friendship and localisation). It reminds us that great civic symbols often belong to all humanity, not just one city.

audience.title: Who Finds Their Resonance Here? (A Guide for Every Visitor)
audience.subtitle: Every visitor can find the way in that suits them best.

items.resonance: Free, open and safe seaside promenade where children can run, take photos and meet this world-famous statue up close.
items.tip: Pair with Aqua City and DiverCity family facilities — mall first, then a relaxed waterfront walk.

items.resonance: At dusk and night, Lady Liberty with the Rainbow Bridge is Odaiba's most romantic scene and highly photogenic.
items.tip: Claim the right-side waterfront platform 30 minutes before dusk; shoot in the blue hour to capture both lights and sky.

items.resonance: Odaiba is a classic filming location for works like Digimon and 20th Century Boys, and next door stands DiverCity's Unicorn Gundam.
items.tip: Route the Statue of Liberty, Unicorn Gundam and Fuji TV together for a 'Odaiba otaku pilgrimage'.

items.resonance: Pose with Lady Liberty without flying to New York; right by Tokyo Bay and the Rainbow Bridge, it is a perfect starting point to discover Tokyo's waterfront.
items.tip: Take the Yurikamome from Shimbashi — the moment it crosses the Rainbow Bridge is a great preview; then walk from the station.

location.welcome: Welcome to Statue of Liberty Odaiba, widely recognized as the central Statue of Liberty. Located in the heart of Minato City, Tokyo, Japan, this destination serves as a primary hub for travellers visiting the region.
location.howToTitle: Location & How to Visit the Statue of Liberty in Minato City
location.howToText: The Statue of Liberty Odaiba stands at 1 Chome-4-2 Daiba, Minato City, Tokyo 135-0091, Japan, at the end of the seaside promenade in Odaiba Kaihin Park. From Shimbashi Station take the Yurikamome about 15 minutes to Daiba Station, then walk roughly 5 minutes; from Tokyo Teleport Station on the Rinkai Line it is about a 10-minute flat walk.

location.landmarksTitle: Landmarks & Attractions Around the Statue of Liberty
location.landmarksIntro: When visiting Statue of Liberty Odaiba, visitors can easily explore surrounding historical landmarks and points of interest, including Rainbow Bridge and Fuji Television Headquarters.

landmarks.name: Rainbow Bridge
landmarks.alt: Rainbow Bridge near the Statue of Liberty Odaiba
landmarks.desc: A 798-metre suspension bridge spanning Tokyo Bay. Stand at the waterfront just to the right of the statue to frame the red-and-white bridge together with the verdigris-green figure — Odaiba's signature postcard view.

landmarks.name: Fuji Television Headquarters
landmarks.alt: Fuji Television Headquarters near the Statue of Liberty
landmarks.desc: The futuristic broadcaster headquarters designed by architect Kenzo Tange, about a 10-minute walk from the statue. Its 25th-floor observation deck offers a full view of Tokyo Bay and the Odaiba waterfront.

tidePage.title: Odaiba Tide Forecast
tidePage.subtitle: The Statue of Liberty stands on a rocky base in Tokyo Bay, where the water rises and falls twice a day. Check the tide before you go to pick the most impressive stretch of water, the best reflections, and the safest hours.
tidePage.chartTitle: Tide level for the next 48 hours
tidePage.chartNote: Predicted water level relative to mean sea level (metres). For reference only; actual conditions on site may differ.

tips.bestText: Around one to two hours either side of high tide the water is at its highest, giving the statue its most dramatic setting against Tokyo Bay. At low tide the rocks around the base emerge and add depth to the scene.
tips.photoText: In calm weather near high tide the surface is smoothest and reflections are complete. Just after sunset, a mid-to-high water level makes it easiest to capture clean water together with the city lights.
tips.safetyText: Rocks and breakwaters exposed at low tide are slippery and are quickly covered again as the water rises. Stay on the promenade, do not go below the waterline, and do not climb the sea wall.

tidePage.disclaimer: Tides are astronomical predictions; air pressure, wind and local terrain can shift actual conditions. Please leave some margin in your plans.

timeline.title: Timeline: The Statue of Liberty in Odaiba
timeline.subtitle: From the creation of the original in New York to the permanent installation on Tokyo Bay — the story in chronological order.

items.title: The original is unveiled in New York
items.text: The original Statue of Liberty, a gift from France marking the centenary of American independence, was installed on Liberty Island in New York Harbour. Its thin copper skin supported by an internal iron framework was designed by Gustave Eiffel, later the engineer of the Eiffel Tower.

items.title: The 'Year of France' brings the replica to Odaiba
items.text: As part of the 'Year of France in Japan', a 1/7-scale replica was installed on the seaside promenade of Odaiba Kaihin Park. It was originally intended as a temporary exhibit for the duration of the event.

items.title: Removal postponed
items.text: The statue was due to be taken down when the event ended, but in response to visitors and local voices who wanted it kept, the installation was extended.

items.title: Permanent installation confirmed
items.text: It became an officially permanent monument and settled into its role as one of the defining landmarks of the Tokyo waterfront.

items.title: A classic Tokyo Bay photo spot
items.text: Framing the statue together with the Rainbow Bridge became widely known, and the view began appearing in travel guides and local publicity.

items.title: A free, 24-hour public space
items.text: As part of the park it is open to anyone, and it offers a different face at every hour — the quiet water at dawn, blue sky at midday and illumination at night.

timeline.note: This timeline is compiled from information published by public bodies, the operator and official tourism sites. Please refer to primary sources for exact dates.

legends.title: Six stories that change how you see the statue
legends.subtitle: The Statue of Liberty is more than a large figure — it is a monument full of meaning. Here we look at how it was made, the symbolism hidden in its details, and how it came to stay in Odaiba.
legends.imageAlt: Detail of the Statue of Liberty Odaiba, Minato City, Tokyo
legends.imageCaption: Step closer and look up: the rays of the crown and the chain at her feet are details most people miss from a distance.

facts.label: Made
facts.value: A replica produced in France based on Bartholdi's original

items.title: Why 1/7 scale?
items.text: The original figure is about 46 m tall and reaches roughly 93 m including its pedestal. The Odaiba statue is about 12.25 m including the pedestal — approximately one seventh of the original. The ratio is said to have been chosen to suit transport, installation and the scale of the park.

items.title: The engineer behind the skin: Eiffel
items.text: The internal iron framework of the original was designed by Gustave Eiffel, later the engineer of the Eiffel Tower. That light structure — a thin copper skin carried by an internal skeleton — is what makes it possible to raise a statue this large in a windy harbour. The Odaiba replica follows the same principle.

items.title: What the chain at her feet means
items.text: A broken chain lies at the statue's feet. It is understood to represent liberation from slavery, and it is the most direct message built into the name 'Liberty'. It is also one of the details most visitors miss when looking up from the front.

items.title: The date inscribed on the tablet
items.text: The tablet held in her left arm is inscribed 'JULY IV MDCCLXXVI' — Roman numerals for 4 July 1776, the date of the American Declaration of Independence. The reading of 'JULY IV' as 'the fourth of July' is one of the most repeated pieces of trivia about the statue.

items.title: The seven rays of the crown
items.text: The seven spikes radiating from the crown are said to represent the seven seas and seven continents, or the spread of liberty's light across the world. The statue standing in Japan carries the very same crown.

items.title: Meant to be temporary — but it stayed
items.text: The Odaiba statue was originally an exhibit for a single event, the 'Year of France'. When its removal was announced, so many people wanted it kept that it remained on the Tokyo waterfront — a story that says a lot about how the city took it to heart.
